answers.rationale: Continuous (iteration-level) batching: at each model-forward iteration the scheduler rebuilds the batch, new requests can join and finished requests can leave without waiting for whole batch.

A: continuous batching removes HOL blocking under variable-length outputs — correct. D: throughput improves aggregate; per-request TPOT (vs running alone at batch-1) may slightly increase due to interference — correct. B wrong: joining a batch does not necessarily reduce single-request TPOT below batch-1 baseline; batching helps aggregate throughput. C wrong: continuous batching applies to dense transformers, not MoE-only.

Chunked prefill splits long prefill into chunks that co-schedule with ongoing decode iterations, avoiding HOL blocking of decode by long prefills. B wrong (activation memory is not the primary motivation). C wrong (not context parallelism). D wrong (tensor-core tile size is not the primary motivation).

CUDA Graphs amortize per-kernel launch overhead by capturing + replaying; shape/layout must match capture, batch composition changes require different graphs or fallback. A/B wrong (no automatic fusion or reordering). C wrong (memory-bound workloads with many small kernels also benefit from removing launch gaps).

Weight-read at ~2000 GB/s ≈ A100 peak → memory-BW-bound. A: continuous batching amortizes weight read across requests — correct. C: 10% launch gaps eliminated by CUDA graph — correct. D: INT4 quant reduces weight bytes ~4x — correct. B wrong: low SM util is symptom of BW-bound, not compute undersubscription.

A: P99 TTFT >> P50 + preemption rate → queueing/HOL. B: decode 25% SM util is BW-bound signature. D: 85% KV usage + preemption → batch limited by KV memory; MQA/GQA/quant/shorter ctx help. C wrong: prefill 92% util suggests compute-bound, and increasing batch would help throughput not fix BW bottleneck (which isn't present in prefill).

A: KV transfer floor on TTFT; needs high-BW interconnect — correct. C: decode nodes shielded from prefill interruption; improves TPOT — correct. B wrong: KV still needed. D wrong: disaggregation typically requires MORE GPUs (each pool sized independently for its SLA) not fewer.
Standard disaggregation motivation: prefill compute-bound, decode BW-bound; separate pools provisioned independently to avoid interference; cost is per-request KV transfer.
Classic HOL blocking under static/dynamic batching; continuous (iteration-level) batching lets short requests exit and new join per iteration.
EP: experts on different devices, all-to-all for routing. SP: shard along sequence axis inside TP region with AllGather/ReduceScatter around sharded region. A correct.

A: fair queueing prevents monopolization — correct. B: chunked prefill interleaves B's long prefills with A's decode — correct. D: per-tenant KV quota — correct. C wrong: serializing tenants would collapse aggregate throughput.
Textbook external fragmentation from contiguous per-sequence slabs sized to max_new_tokens; PagedAttention solves this.
Standard production fusion set: fused QKV, fused RMSNorm, fused SwiGLU, fused attention (FA/PagedAttn), fused sampling.
Per-token KV = 2 * L * H_kv * d * 2B = 2*32*8*128*2 = 131,072 B ≈ 128 KB. 46 GB / 128 KB ≈ 376,832 tokens. At 2000 tokens/seq ≈ 188 seqs. C correct.
A: attention read time grows linearly with context; rivals weight read — correct. C: KV grows linearly, halves batch — correct. B/D wrong.

B: KV quant ~2x — correct. C: reduce batch cap trades throughput for less preemption — correct. D: prefix caching reduces per-request KV for shared prefixes — correct. A wrong: PP replicates weights but each stage still stores its own layers' KV entries for the SEQ that flows through it; PP doesn't multiply KV capacity per stage — PP would put a subset of layers on each GPU, so KV capacity for those layers per GPU can grow (fewer layers per GPU), but claim '8x more KV capacity per pipeline stage' is misleading and 'pipeline parallelism REPLICATES KV cache' is false.
Standard PagedAttention: fixed-size blocks + per-sequence block table; eliminates external frag and internal reservation.
PagedAttention: per-block table lookup then load block into SMEM; same online softmax math as FA; extra cost is small per-block lookup, not per-element.

A: block sharing enables prefix caching and beam search — correct. C: compatible with FA-style tiled softmax — correct. D: fixed-size blocks; internal waste bounded by block_size-1 — correct. B wrong: paging is not compression.
Prefill (P tokens processed together) is compute-bound; decode (batch-1) is BW-bound because linear layers become GEMV with intensity ~1 flop/byte.
PP partitions layers across P devices; per-request latency not reduced; multiple in-flight requests amortize; imbalance causes bubbles. Only A is correct.
Prefix caching stores KV blocks of prior tokens; exact reuse requires token-identical prefix; reduces/eliminates prefill of shared prefix.
Standard vLLM behavior: preempt (drop-and-recompute or swap-to-host) to admit new prefills; resume when capacity available.

Given the profile data arithmetic in the stem: expected ~3.94 accepted tokens per 20 ms verification = 0.20 tok/ms vs baseline 0.10 tok/ms → speedup ≈ 2x. Acceptance p dominates; upper bound as p→1 is (k+1)/(1+draft_cost_frac*(k+1)).
Standard spec dec: small draft proposes k tokens autoregressively; target runs single forward on all k; rejection sampling accepts prefix with target's exact distribution.

B: most beneficial when target is memory-BW-bound (batch-1 decode) — correct. D: rejection sampling preserves target distribution exactly — correct. A wrong: speedup depends on acceptance rate and draft cost. C wrong: draft and target need not share weights.
Megatron-LM TP: column-parallel W_up (each device 1/T of intermediate cols), row-parallel W_down (each device 1/T rows); single AllReduce per MLP and per attention block to sum partial outputs.
TPOT = avg wall time between consecutive output tokens after the first; excludes TTFT. Total latency ≈ TTFT + (M-1)*TPOT.
TTFT = arrival to first-token delivery (~210 ms), dominated by 182 ms prefill of 1024-token prompt; mitigation: chunked prefill, prefix cache, TP.

A: after transition to compute-bound, throughput sees diminishing returns while TPOT rises — correct. C: batch amortizes weight reads (throughput up), per-step time slightly longer (TPOT up mildly) — correct. B/D wrong.
